text: Neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) models replace discrete hidden-state updates with learned continuous dynamics evaluated by a numerical solver. Adjoint sensitivities compute gradients through a reverse-time augmented ODE without retaining intermediate solver operations, making memory independent of function-evaluation count while tolerances control the precision-computation trade-off. On MNIST, 0.42% error with 0.22 million parameters versus a residual network's 0.41% with 0.60 million supports parameter-efficient classification, not improved accuracy. For dynamics uniformly Lipschitz in state and continuous in time, an instantaneous change-of-variables theorem replaces the Jacobian determinant with a trace in log-density evolution. Trace additivity permits continuous normalizing flows whose density-update cost is linear in hidden-unit count per function evaluation; two-dimensional experiments illustrate density matching and reversible sampling. A latent ODE generates states at irregular observation times from an initial state and shared continuous dynamics, and can incorporate a Poisson likelihood for observation times. On synthetic noisy spirals using 30 of 100 observations, predictive RMSE is 0.1642 versus 0.3937 for an RNN over 100 prediction times extending beyond training observations, supporting reconstruction and extrapolation in this setting. Reverse-time trajectory reconstruction can introduce numerical error; checkpointing can mitigate it by storing intermediate states.

FlexGen addresses bulk language-model inference when weights and key-value caches exceed GPU memory. Offloading weights, activations, and caches across GPU, CPU, and disk permits larger batches; processing multiple batches with each loaded layer amortizes weight transfers. An analytical cost model and linear-programming search select placements and batch sizes. Without CPU computation and neglecting activation I/O, asymptotic weight transfers are within twice optimal. Group-wise 4-bit compression without retraining or calibration further reduces transfers, allowing OPT-175B to avoid disk swapping. In dummy-weight benchmarks with 512-token prompts and 32-token outputs, a 16-GB T4 with 208-GB host memory and SSD achieves 0.69 generated tokens/s, or 1.12 compressed, versus 0.01 for unquantized Accelerate and DeepSpeed. This comparison supports greater bulk throughput through weight reuse and expanded batching, not low-latency generation. Separate real-weight Lambada and WikiText tests show small quality changes with 4-bit compression and sparse value-cache loading; 3-bit compression fails to preserve accuracy, and compression can reduce throughput on smaller models. Four-GPU pipelining scales decoding superlinearly, but total generation scales sublinearly for OPT-30B and OPT-175B with 32-token outputs. The benefits therefore depend on substantial host memory and throughput-oriented workloads.

FlexGen targets batched large language model inference when weights and key-value caches exceed GPU memory. Block scheduling reuses loaded weights across GPU batches, while cache offloading permits larger batches; a cost model and linear programming select tensor placement across GPU, CPU, and disk. Without CPU computation, idealized asymptotic weight I/O stays within twice the optimum. In dummy-weight benchmarks with 512-token prompts and 32 generated tokens, OPT-175B on one 16-GB T4, 208-GB CPU memory, and a 1.5-TB SSD reaches 0.69 tokens/s versus 0.01 for uncompressed Accelerate and DeepSpeed. These gains accompany larger effective batches that amortize loaded weights across more prompts. Four-bit weight and cache compression without retraining or calibration raises throughput to 1.12 tokens/s by fitting tensors in CPU memory and avoiding disk swapping. Separate real-weight tests show small Lambada accuracy and WikiText perplexity changes, including sparse value-cache access, but compression can slow models fitting GPU memory. With four GPUs, offloaded models show super-linear decoding scaling but sublinear overall scaling when generating 32 tokens. Seven HELM sub-scenarios with OPT-IML-30B finish in 21 hours including overhead, establishing batch utility under long completion times and substantial host-memory and storage requirements.

Neural ordinary differential equations define hidden states by learned continuous dynamics evaluated with an ODE solver. Rather than retaining solver operations, adjoint training reconstructs the trajectory while solving an augmented ODE backward, making memory independent of function evaluations. Solver tolerances trade numerical accuracy against computation. For dynamics uniformly Lipschitz in state and continuous in time, an instantaneous change-of-variables theorem makes log-density evolution depend on the dynamics' Jacobian trace rather than a transformation determinant. Because traces add, continuous normalizing flows can increase additive hidden-unit width with linear density-update cost. Toy density experiments illustrate reversible sampling and density estimation. A latent-trajectory model evaluates states at arbitrary observation times without time binning and can jointly model observation timing with a Poisson likelihood. On MNIST, 0.42% error with 0.22 million parameters versus a residual network's 0.41% with 0.60 million supports comparable classification performance with fewer parameters. On synthetic spirals with 30 irregularly sampled observations, predictive RMSE of 0.1642 versus an RNN's 0.3937 supports extrapolation beyond training observation times. Backward reconstruction can introduce numerical error; checkpointing trades additional storage for reconstruction accuracy.
